cause: Bacteria that spread through splashing water, infected seed or transplants, and handling wet plants.
what_to_do_now: Remove and bag badly spotted leaves; avoid working among wet plants; switch from overhead to drip or base watering.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants; rotate away from pepper and tomato for 2-3 years; clean tools between plants.
when_to_seek_help: If spots spread to new leaves or fruit within days, or the crop is commercial. Ask the extension office about locally approved treatments.
source_name: Cornell Vegetable MD Online (general vegetable disease reference)

cause: A fungus (Alternaria) that favours warm, humid weather and attacks older leaves first, producing ringed brown spots.
what_to_do_now: Remove heavily infected lower leaves; keep foliage dry; avoid overhead watering late in the day.
prevention: Rotate crops; remove plant debris after harvest; use healthy seed tubers; keep plants well fed and watered.
when_to_seek_help: If lesions keep spreading upward or the field is large. Fungicide choice and timing should follow local extension advice.
source_name: UC IPM tomato early blight page (same pathogen group; used as a reference)

cause: A fungus-like water mold (Phytophthora infestans) that spreads very fast in cool, wet weather and can infect tubers.
what_to_do_now: Act quickly: remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost); avoid overhead watering; do not store suspect tubers with healthy ones.
prevention: Use healthy seed tubers; hill soil over tubers; improve airflow; scout often in cool wet spells.
when_to_seek_help: Immediately, since this disease can destroy a crop in days. Contact the local extension office or agriculture department.
source_name: UMass Extension tomato leaf blights fact sheet (late blight covered for tomato and potato)

cause: A fungus (Alternaria) favoured by warm, wet weather; it starts on lower leaves as spots with concentric rings.
what_to_do_now: Remove infected lower leaves; mulch to stop soil splash; keep leaves dry; water at the base.
prevention: Rotate crops; clear plant debris after harvest; stake plants for airflow; choose tolerant varieties where available.
when_to_seek_help: If it climbs the plant or reaches fruit. Fungicide choice and timing should follow local extension advice.

cause: A fungus-like water mold (Phytophthora infestans) that spreads very fast in cool, wet weather on leaves, stems and fruit.
what_to_do_now: Act quickly: remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost); avoid overhead watering; isolate from healthy plants and nearby potatoes.
prevention: Use healthy transplants; improve airflow; scout often in cool wet spells.
when_to_seek_help: Immediately, since it can destroy plants in days. Contact the local extension office or agriculture department.
source_name: UMass Extension tomato leaf blights fact sheet

cause: A fungus that thrives in high humidity and poor airflow, common in greenhouses and high tunnels; shows as yellow patches above and olive mold below.
what_to_do_now: Improve ventilation and lower humidity; remove affected leaves; avoid wetting foliage.
prevention: Space and prune plants for airflow; water at the base in the morning; choose resistant varieties where available.
when_to_seek_help: If it keeps spreading despite better ventilation. Ask the extension office for local options.
source_name: Cornell Vegetable MD Online tomato diagnostic key

cause: A fungus (Septoria) spread by splashing water; it makes many small tan spots with dark edges, starting on lower leaves.
what_to_do_now: Remove infected lower leaves; mulch to stop soil splash; keep leaves dry.
prevention: Rotate crops for 2 years; clear plant debris; water at the base; stake plants.
when_to_seek_help: If many leaves are spotted or it moves up the plant. Fungicide choice and timing should follow local extension advice.
source_name: University of Kentucky early blight and Septoria leaf spot fact sheet

cause: Tiny sap-sucking mites that build up in hot, dry, dusty conditions; leaves look speckled or bronzed, sometimes with fine webbing.
what_to_do_now: Check the underside of leaves for mites; rinse plants with a firm water spray; reduce dust around plants.
prevention: Avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen; keep plants watered; protect natural predators by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.
when_to_seek_help: If speckling spreads or webbing appears. Ask the extension office about locally approved miticides.
source_name: Cornell Vegetable MD Online (general vegetable pest reference)

cause: A fungus (Corynespora) favoured by warm, humid conditions; causes brown spots with ring patterns on leaves and fruit.
what_to_do_now: Remove infected leaves; improve airflow by pruning and spacing; keep leaves dry.
prevention: Rotate crops; clear plant debris; water at the base; avoid dense planting.
when_to_seek_help: If lesions spread to new leaves or fruit. Fungicide choice and timing should follow local extension advice.
source_name: Cornell Vegetable MD Online tomato diagnostic key

cause: A virus spread by whiteflies; leaves curl upward and turn yellow, and plants stay stunted. There is no cure.
what_to_do_now: Remove and destroy infected plants early; control whiteflies; remove nearby weeds.
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties; protect seedlings with insect-proof netting; use reflective mulch; inspect transplants.
when_to_seek_help: As soon as symptoms appear, so the virus does not spread. Ask the extension office about whitefly control.
source_name: Cornell Vegetable MD Online (general vegetable virus reference)

cause: A virus that spreads on hands, tools and seed; leaves show mottled light and dark green patches and may be distorted. There is no cure.
what_to_do_now: Remove and destroy infected plants; wash hands and clean tools after handling them; do not handle healthy plants after infected ones.
prevention: Use clean seed and resistant varieties; sanitise tools; avoid handling tobacco before touching plants.
when_to_seek_help: As soon as symptoms appear, so the virus does not spread. Ask the extension office for local advice.
source_name: Cornell Vegetable MD Online (general vegetable virus reference)
